newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSIGHT - Aussie tenses for "good" inflation news.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Aussie tenses for "good" inflation news.

text.p: *AUD drifted off overnight, being ignored by offshore markets more concerned with Greenspan and a surge in US$/mark *Market braced for consumer price data at 11.30 am which are expected to show Q2 underlying inflation close to record lows
*Benign figures would be seen as green light for an RBA easing, perhaps as early as Friday, and see AUD pressured
Such a crossover would be almost unprecedented and dealers suspect offshore investors would react by dumping the A$ in favour of higher yielders like the U.S. dollar.
By 8.15 am (2215 GMT) the local dollar was tensed at US$0.7389/94 having drifted off from a US$0.7423 offhsore high and US$0.7400/05 late here Tuesday.

Traders said the currency was largely ignored by overseas markets who were busy trashing the mark -- the A$ surged to 1.3470/83 marks from 1.3356/69 -- and celebrating a cautiously upbeat testimony from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan in which he implied a policy tightening was unlikely for now.
That was supportive of the A$ in that a U.S. hike would have further widened the US$'s interest differential, but also removed a potential impediment to another easing here.
The forex market is probably more sceptical than the bond and futures markets about whether the RBA will cut but has still pushed the dollar down on a "just in case" basis.

The A$ fell three cents in response to the last easing on May 23, steadied around 75 cents for a while and then slid to 73 when poor economic data suggested another easing was on the way. It bounced from this oversold position but could well return to those 18-month lows if today's data are as weak as some expect.

Underlying inflation is expected to rise 0.4 percent on the quarter taking annual growth to just 1.7 percent, the lowest level in 27 years and crucially below the RBA's target band of 2-3 percent. Headline CPI should fall 0.1 peercent leaving the annual rate at 0.5 percent from 1.3 percent in Q1.
Analysts reckon the RBA would be hard pressed not to cut in the face of such favourable numbers and, as long as wages data Thursday were as benign as expected, could move Friday morning.
The crucial question for the A$ would be how much of the easing had the market already priced in. Dealers were uncertain, but most answered "not all". -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
